newsitem.title: ITALY: Rwanda calls for Zaire force to be scrapped.
newsitem.headline: Rwanda calls for Zaire force to be scrapped.

text.p: Rwanda called on Saturday for a U.N.-sanctioned force for eastern Zaire to be scrapped, while neighbouring Burundi said the troops being sent should do more than just help with aid deliveries to starving refugees.

As Western and African troops prepared to move in, Rwandan Prime Minister Pierre Celestin Rwigema told the World Food Summit in Rome that aid should go to his country and that money for the force should be spent on resettling refugees at home.
Hundreds of thousands of Rwandan Hutu refugees, stranded in eastern Zaire, have been streaming home since Friday.

But the United Nations says the multinational force is still needed as some refugees from Rwanda and Burundi remain. Most of them fled to Zaire in 1994 after the massacre in Rwanda of some 800,000 people, mainly rival Tutsis, and fighting in Burundi.

"The Rwandan government appeals to the international community to move aid for these refugees to Rwanda and to use the budget for the deployment of the force to resettle and reintegrate these people," Rwigema told the summit.
The U.N. Security Council, which approved the force, should now look again at the situation, he added.

Burundi's Prime Minister Pascal Firmin Ndimira said the multinational force -- expected to number as many as 10,000 troops -- should be more actively involved in moving remaining refugees back to Rwanda and Burundi, not simply help with aid.
"The only realistic solution is that all refugees return home," he told a news conference.
Zaire has accused Rwanda and Burundi of stoking the crisis on its territory and a Zairean envoy said on Friday his country was ready for war with both neighbours.

Burundi's Ndimira dismissed the comments from Zairean Deputy Foreign Minister Lokondo Yoka, saying that Burundi was not directly involved in the crisis and that no evidence had been produced to show that it was.
"Is Burundi in conflict with Zaire? I would say no," he said.
Amid the confusion in central Africa, a senior European official at the Rome summit also criticised plans for the multinational force, saying its mandate was inadequate.
European Commissioner for Humanitarian Aid Emma Bonino told a news conference the troops should have been given authority to disarm and separate Hutu militia groups from the refugees.
Those groups, which exerted a powerful hold over the refugees and dissuaded them from returning home until this week, are widely believed to include people involved in the 1994 genocide in Rwanda.
Without that power, Bonino said aid workers were exposed to danger which could hinder efforts to feed refugees and organise safe passage to their homes in Rwanda and Burundi.

"The mandate of the force...remains unsatisfactory and probably insufficient in as much as it does not include the aim of disarming refugees and separating remaining military elements therein," she said.
"How can aid agencies operate once more in an environment under threat by not only one but many armed militias in the region?" she asked.
